title: US Moves to Strip Citizenship From 40 People in Largest Denaturalization Push Yet
excerpt: The Justice Department filed 40 denaturalization cases between Aug. 21 and Oct. 2 against naturalized citizens accused of serious crimes and immigration fraud — the biggest such push in modern US history.
body:
• The Justice Department filed denaturalization actions in federal courts against 40 naturalized US citizens between August 21 and October 2, 2026 — the largest single-period batch of such filings under the Trump administration.
  • Attorney General Todd Blanche called it "the largest denaturalization effort in modern history." The defendants are accused of crimes including espionage, voluntary manslaughter, aggravated sodomy, sexual abuse of minors, and immigration fraud.
  • One Indian national is on the list: Balwinder Singh, 55, accused of using two identities — applying for immigration benefits in 1992 under one identity, gaining permanent residence under a second in 2003, and naturalizing in 2009. The DOJ filed the complaint on September 8 in California.
  • What this means for you: denaturalization applies only to naturalized citizens whose citizenship was illegally procured or obtained by concealing material facts — not to natural-born citizens or those who naturalized honestly. USCIS form N-400 asks applicants under oath whether they have committed crimes; false answers are the basis of many of these cases. Researchers at the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRACE) found this six-week batch exceeds the past several years of denaturalization filings combined, and expect the pace to continue.

The US Justice Department on Monday announced denaturalization actions against 40 naturalized citizens in the largest such effort in modern American history. The complaints were filed in multiple federal district courts between August 21 and October 2, 2026, and represent the largest volume of denaturalization filings in a single period under the Trump administration, according to the department.

"Today's announcement marks the largest denaturalization effort in modern history."

— Todd Blanche, US Attorney General

Who the cases target

The 40 defendants, ages 26 to 76, come from countries around the world, with Mexico accounting for the most (11). The allegations span espionage, voluntary manslaughter, aggravated sodomy against a special-needs man, transportation of child pornography, and sexual abuse of minors — but not all involve violent crime. According to USA Today, at least 25 of the 40 face proceedings for reasons related to lying on visa or naturalization forms.

https://x.com/Newsforce/status/2107242428423963029

Among the most serious cases: Jinchao Wei, a 26-year-old China-born former US Navy sailor convicted of espionage-related offenses, who enlisted in 2021, began selling military secrets to China by February 2022, and became a US citizen in May 2022 under expedited military naturalization provisions. Another case involves Balwinder Singh, 55, an Indian national accused of using a fraudulent dual identity across two decades — applying for immigration benefits in 1992 under one identity, obtaining permanent residence under a second in 2003, and naturalizing in 2009, with fingerprints tying the two applications together. Other defendants include Ahmed Khan, accused of using a bogus death certificate for his living Pakistani wife to obtain a green card, and Iain Lumsden of the United Kingdom, convicted of transporting child pornography after falsely swearing he had committed no unreported crimes.

The legal basis

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, a naturalized citizen's citizenship can be revoked if the naturalization was illegally procured or obtained by concealment of a material fact or willful misrepresentation. "This administration will continue to pursue the largest denaturalization effort in department history to restore trust and integrity in US citizenship," said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department's Civil Division.

Denaturalization was once a rarity in federal courts — an average of just 11 cases a year between 1990 and 2017, according to New York Times reporting. That is changing fast. Researchers at the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRACE) said this batch amounts to more than the past several years combined, and wrote in a June report that "denaturalization, once a rare occurrence in federal courts, is now becoming increasingly common. This increase is expected to continue."

Why it matters to Indian immigrants

For the Indian diaspora, this is not an abstract enforcement statistic. Indians are among the largest nationalities seeking US citizenship — and one Indian national is already named among the 40. The message from the administration is explicit: deception during the naturalization process, however far back, can be pursued years later. For green-card holders preparing N-400 applications, the practical takeaway is unglamorous but consequential — answer every question on the form completely and honestly, disclose anything questionable, and consult an immigration attorney if your record has any complications. A single concealed fact can unravel citizenship decades after it was granted.

What's next

The 40 complaints are now before federal judges across the country, and denaturalization requires the government to prove its case in court — the defendants remain US citizens until a judge rules otherwise. Some will fight: the attorney for Walid Osman, a 62-year-old Egyptian native accused of lying on naturalization forms, told USA Today the filing was "riddled with errors and speculation," adding, "He's a US citizen, and we're going to fight to keep it that way." But the administration's direction is unambiguous. With the DOJ promising to continue the largest denaturalization effort in its history and enforcement resources expanding, naturalized citizens with any irregularity in their history should assume the scrutiny is only beginning.
image_caption: A U.S. passport. The government has moved to strip citizenship from 40 people in the largest denaturalization drive in decades.
nri_angle: One Indian national is named among the 40 denaturalization targets, and the sweeping push puts the large Indian naturalized population and N-400 applicants on notice that concealment on immigration forms — however old — can now trigger loss of citizenship.
